findings.title: A running daemon does not reload newly written setup configuration
findings.detail: Service installation is skipped whenever the preflight daemon check is healthy, even when init just wrote new providers, repositories, or merge policy. The service therefore continues using its old in-memory configuration. The partial-config test mocks the service and checks the file rather than the daemon's effective settings.
findings.suggestion: Reload or restart the service when configuration changes, and test init against a fake service that retains its loaded configuration until reloaded.
findings.failure_scenario: A healthy daemon is running when init adds a provider and changes the merge default; init reports success, but subsequent daemon operations still use the old configuration.

verification.evidence: src/cli/setup.ts:203 writes configuration, but :207-208 calls `d.install()` only when the preflight daemon status is not `ok`. src/cli/main.ts:160-165 loads configuration once with `const cfg = loadConfig()` and constructs `new Factory(cfg, ...)`. src/app.ts:81-86 captures the catalog and provider definitions from that configuration.
verification.trigger: Run init against a healthy daemon at the installed SHA while adding a provider or filling the missing merge default. Config is written, but service installation/restart is skipped, leaving daemon operations on the previous providers and merge policy until restart.

findings.title: Init tests replace the production smoke adapter
findings.detail: The fixture substitutes `d.smoke` with a fixed passing row, so the tests do not exercise the production adapter, its use of the configured paths and environment, or collection of actual smoke failures. This leaves the central requirement to run live smoke checks unverified.
findings.suggestion: Add a test of the production smoke adapter with fake CLI and HTTP dependencies, verifying that real collected failures appear in the summary and produce a nonzero exit.
findings.failure_scenario: The production smoke adapter stops collecting rows or runs with the wrong configuration; every init test still receives the fixture's fixed passing result.

verification.evidence: test/setup-support.ts:65–68 replaces the adapter with `d.smoke = async () => { effects.push("smoke"); return [{ name: "live", status: "pass", durationMs: 1 }]; };`. test/init.test.ts:9 uses `setupFixture()`. The production adapter at src/cli/setup.ts:269 calls `main(() => {}, { onRow: (row) => rows.push(row) })`, which these init tests never exercise.
verification.trigger: A regression in the production smoke adapter's row collection or configuration remains undetected by the init tests because their fixture supplies a fixed passing row.

findings.title: Redact smoke retry details before they are truncated
findings.detail: Smoke rows are redacted only after the smoke runner has constructed retriedAfter by truncating the first failure reason to 200 characters. If truncation cuts through a credential, safe() cannot match the complete credential, and the remaining fragment is written to smoke-last.json and printed in the init summary.
findings.suggestion: Redact failure reasons before constructing or truncating retry details, including the first-attempt reason.
findings.failure_scenario: A transient smoke failure includes a configured API key near the 200-character boundary. The retry succeeds, but retriedAfter contains a partial key that is persisted and returned by init.

verification.evidence: scripts/smoke.ts:282 truncates first: `retriedAfter: (first ?? "failed").replace(/\s+/g, " ").trim().slice(0, 200)`. src/cli/setup.ts:25 subsequently redacts only complete values: `text = text.replaceAll(value, "[redacted]")`; :221 persists the encoded smoke rows. However, src/harness/claude.ts:363 already feeds parser output through `redactCredentials`, and src/util/proc.ts:285 redacts registered secrets of at least eight characters, so ordinary credential-bearing CLI errors have an earlier guard.
verification.trigger: If a smoke failure reason reaches retry handling with an unredacted configured key crossing character 200, truncation leaves a key prefix that setup's complete-value replacement cannot remove. That prefix is persisted and printed; a production path supplying that unredacted reason is not established.

findings.title: Check access to repositories supplied to init
findings.detail: Doctor checks repository access only for the first repository already present in the loaded configuration. The --repo values are processed after doctor finishes, so a fresh init can accept and enable repositories without checking access to any of them. Additional configured repositories are also never checked.
findings.suggestion: Validate access for every repository that init will enable before writing configuration, and report each configured repository's access in doctor.
findings.failure_scenario: On a fresh configuration, `limitless init --yes --repo org/private` passes gh auth status even though the account lacks access or SSO authorization for org/private, then writes that repository into configuration.

verification.evidence: src/cli/setup.ts:129 runs `const checks = await doctor(d)` before processing flags. Doctor selects only existing configuration at :57: `const repo = (d.config.raw.github as { repos?: string[] } | undefined)?.repos?.[0]`; :58 guards repository access with `if (ghOk && repo)`. Requested repositories appear later at :189: `const requested = flags.repo ?? parsed.filter(Boolean)`, and :203 writes config without another access check.
verification.trigger: On empty config, authenticated `init --yes --repo org/private` skips the repository read and writes org/private even when access or SSO authorization is missing.

findings.title: Discreet mode is never offered or configured
findings.detail: The request says init asks about “the merge policy, and discreet mode.” The implementation always reports discreet mode as skipped and never asks or persists a choice.
findings.suggestion: Implement the requested discreet-mode question and configuration, or explicitly revise the requirement if that feature cannot be supported.
findings.failure_scenario: A user runs init on a fresh installation and has no opportunity to select discreet mode.

verification.evidence: src/cli/setup.ts:192 asks only `Merge policy (auto/pr/none)` before assembling configuration. At :223 discreet mode is explicitly replaced with `const discreet = "skipped: discreet mode: not available yet (#37)"`; :224 merely includes that string in the summary.
verification.trigger: A fresh interactive init offers no discreet-mode choice and configures no discreet behavior, leaving the requested privacy protection unavailable.

findings.title: Fresh setup does not verify access to the requested repositories
findings.detail: The request requires gh authentication to have repository access and an SSO read against a configured repository. Doctor checks only the first repository already in config, before init collects --repo or interactive repository choices. A fresh install therefore proceeds without checking any selected repository, and additional configured repositories are never checked.
findings.suggestion: Check access to each repository selected for setup before writing configuration, and report SSO failures with the requested fix.
findings.failure_scenario: An authenticated user runs init --yes --repo org/private on an empty config without access or SSO authorization; the check passes and setup writes the repository anyway.

verification.evidence: src/cli/setup.ts:56 checks `gh auth status`, while :57 reads only `d.config.raw.github...repos?.[0]` and :58 performs a repository read only `if (ghOk && repo)`. At :189–193 the supplied repositories are added to raw configuration, which :203 writes without checking their accessibility.
verification.trigger: An authenticated user supplies an inaccessible or SSO-blocked repository on fresh setup; the absent configured repository bypasses the access probe and setup persists the requested repository. This is the same defect as C20.

findings.title: A healthy daemon is left running with stale configuration
findings.detail: Init writes newly detected providers and repository settings but skips service installation or reload whenever the pre-write doctor saw a healthy daemon. The already running daemon retains its old configuration, so the setup changes do not take effect there.
findings.suggestion: Safely reload or restart the service when configuration affecting the daemon changes, then wait for health before smoke checks.
findings.failure_scenario: Init adds a local provider while the daemon is healthy; subsequent daemon runs cannot route to that provider until the service is restarted separately.

findings.title: OpenAI model lists can be misclassified as Anthropic servers
findings.detail: The detection treats a first model with type equal to model as proof of an Anthropic-compatible API. The OpenAI model object can also contain type: model, so this heuristic can register an OpenAI endpoint with the Anthropic harness and the wrong base URL.
findings.suggestion: Probe an endpoint or response characteristic that reliably distinguishes the supported protocols, and avoid registering an ambiguous server under an unverified protocol.
findings.failure_scenario: A loopback OpenAI-compatible server returns a model list containing {"id":"local","type":"model"}; init registers it as anthropic-compatible and subsequent requests use the wrong protocol.

findings.title: Configured providers without health_url receive no health check
findings.detail: The request says every configured provider answers its health check. This loop silently omits health status whenever health_url is absent, even though that field is optional for configured compatible providers.
findings.suggestion: Provide an appropriate health probe for configured providers or explicitly report that their health cannot be checked with an actionable fix.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured compatible provider has a base URL but no health_url and its server is down; doctor reports no provider health problem.

findings.title: Doctor omits the individual last smoke results
findings.detail: The request says “the last smoke results” are reported. Doctor reduces the stored rows to a pass summary or failed names, omitting individual passed and skipped checks and their reasons.
findings.suggestion: Include the stored smoke rows, including statuses and useful reasons, in human-readable and JSON output.
findings.failure_scenario: The last smoke run skipped a backend because credentials were unavailable; doctor says only that the last smoke passed.

findings.title: --yes changes MCP configuration despite the default being no
findings.detail: The request says --yes accepts defaults and init asks before changing MCP configuration. The confirmation default is false, but confirm returns true unconditionally under --yes, causing both client configurations to be changed without the stated default being respected.
findings.suggestion: Have --yes select the actual confirmation default, or provide a separate explicit opt-in for MCP registration.
findings.failure_scenario: A non-interactive user runs init --yes expecting the default no for MCP registration; init invokes the client MCP add commands.

candidates.title: Configured repositories are never enabled
candidates.detail: Init writes github.repos, but no runtime code consumes that setting to register or enable repositories. The summary reports them as added even though the factory has not enabled them.
candidates.suggestion: Connect the configured repositories to the repository registration or enablement path and cover the resulting runtime behavior.
candidates.failure_scenario: Run init --yes --repo acme/app on a fresh installation; the config contains acme/app, but no repository is registered as a result.

candidates.title: A running daemon does not load the configuration init just wrote
candidates.detail: Service installation is skipped whenever the preflight daemon has the current SHA, even if init just added providers or changed GitHub settings. The daemon loads configuration at startup, so it continues running with its old configuration while init reports success.
candidates.suggestion: Apply configuration changes to the running daemon safely, or restart it through the existing service workflow when changes require a reload.
candidates.failure_scenario: A healthy daemon is running when init adds a local provider; init reports the provider added and service already set, but the daemon continues using its previous provider catalog.

candidates.title: Model metadata is used to infer an incompatible API protocol
candidates.detail: The type field of a model-list entry does not identify the server's inference protocol. In particular, OpenAI-compatible servers can return entries with type model, which this code classifies as Anthropic-compatible and configures with an Anthropic endpoint.
candidates.suggestion: Probe protocol-specific endpoints or ask the user to choose the protocol when it cannot be determined reliably.
candidates.failure_scenario: A local OpenAI-compatible server returns {"data":[{"id":"example","type":"model"}]}; init writes kind anthropic-compatible, so subsequent model requests use the wrong API.

candidates.title: Repository access checks omit newly requested and additional repositories
candidates.detail: Doctor checks only the first repository already present in the config. On a fresh init, --repo values are processed after doctor, so no repository access or SSO check is performed for them. Later repositories are never checked either.
candidates.suggestion: Check access for each configured or newly requested repository before writing configuration, preserving the SSO-specific fix.
candidates.failure_scenario: An authenticated user runs init --yes --repo org/private without SSO authorization; preflight passes without reading that repository and setup proceeds.

candidates.title: Init never asks for or configures discreet mode
candidates.detail: The requested discreet-mode question is replaced by a fixed skipped message. Neither interactive setup nor --yes records a choice, so this portion of the setup command is absent.
candidates.suggestion: Implement the requested question and persist or apply its selected default using the supported configuration mechanism.
candidates.failure_scenario: A user runs interactive init expecting to choose discreet mode; no question is presented and no setting is applied.

candidates.title: --yes overrides the negative MCP registration default
candidates.detail: confirm returns true whenever --yes is supplied, even when its fallback is false. Consequently an unattended init modifies Claude and Codex configuration although the registration prompt's default is no; --yes was specified to accept defaults.
candidates.suggestion: Have --yes select the supplied fallback, including false, and require an explicit affirmative choice or option for MCP registration.
candidates.failure_scenario: Run init --yes --json on a fresh machine with both CLIs installed; MCP registration commands run despite the prompt's no default.

candidates.title: Doctor does not report individual last smoke results
candidates.detail: The stored smoke rows include check names, statuses, and reasons, but doctor reduces them to a single pass message or a list of failed names. Skipped checks and their reasons are hidden, and an entirely skipped run is described as passed.
candidates.suggestion: Report each stored smoke result, including skips and failure reasons, in both text and JSON output.
candidates.failure_scenario: The last smoke run contains only skipped checks because providers were unavailable; doctor reports last smoke passed.

candidates.title: Reload the daemon after writing configuration
candidates.detail: When the daemon was healthy during doctor, init writes new provider or repository settings but skips service installation or restart. The running daemon retains its old configuration, while init reports the service as already set and proceeds to smoke checks.
candidates.suggestion: Reload or restart the service when configuration changes, then verify the new daemon is healthy.
candidates.failure_scenario: Run init against a healthy daemon and add a provider or change the repository list; init succeeds while the daemon continues using the previous configuration.

candidates.title: Check access to every selected repository
candidates.detail: Doctor reads only the first configured repository, and init runs doctor before it collects --repo arguments. Consequently, inaccessible repositories and organization SSO failures can be accepted without inspection.
candidates.suggestion: Check each configured and newly requested repository before writing configuration, and report the repository-specific fix.
candidates.failure_scenario: A fresh `init --yes --repo org/private` has valid gh authentication but no SSO authorization; no repository API read occurs and setup continues.

candidates.title: Treat failed configured-provider health checks as failures
candidates.detail: An unreachable or unhealthy configured provider is classified as a warning, so init proceeds despite the request that it stop on failed doctor checks. The same classification makes doctor return success for an unhealthy provider.
candidates.suggestion: Return a failed check for an unsuccessful configured-provider health check, preserving enough detail to identify the failure.
candidates.failure_scenario: A configured provider's health endpoint returns HTTP 503; doctor exits successfully and init writes configuration and continues.

candidates.title: Do not report skipped smoke checks as passed
candidates.detail: The last smoke result is reported as passed when every row is skipped. This hides the absence of actual live or inspection results and gives doctor a successful status.
candidates.suggestion: Report skipped checks separately and warn when required checks did not run.
candidates.failure_scenario: A stored smoke result contains only skipped checks because prerequisites were unavailable; doctor prints `last smoke passed`.

candidates.title: Honor the default of declining MCP registration
candidates.detail: The confirmation helper returns true unconditionally for --yes, even when its default is false. Thus noninteractive setup changes both CLI configurations without the requested affirmative registration choice.
candidates.suggestion: Have --yes accept the supplied default, including false for MCP registration, or provide an explicit registration flag.
candidates.failure_scenario: `limitless init --yes --json` reaches MCP registration and runs the CLI configuration commands despite the registration prompt's default being no.

candidates.title: Collect and persist the requested discreet-mode setting
candidates.detail: Init always reports discreet mode as unavailable and never asks for or saves the requested setting. The added test explicitly accepts this omission.
candidates.suggestion: Implement the requested discreet-mode question and persist the setting, or explicitly defer the requirement in the request.
candidates.failure_scenario: A user runs interactive init expecting to select discreet mode; setup completes without offering the choice.

candidates.title: Selected repositories are saved but never enabled
candidates.detail: Init writes the selected names to `github.repos`, but no runtime code consumes that setting to register or enable repositories. The init test checks only the serialized configuration, so it passes even though the requested setup has no operational effect.
candidates.suggestion: Register or otherwise enable the selected repositories, and add an integration test that verifies they are available to the running service after init.
candidates.failure_scenario: A fresh installation runs `limitless init --yes --repo acme/app`; the configuration lists `acme/app`, but the service has not registered that repository.

candidates.title: Test asserts that discreet-mode setup is skipped
candidates.detail: The request requires init to ask about discreet mode, but the implementation always returns a hard-coded unavailable message. The empty-init test explicitly expects that message, making the unmet behavior pass as intended.
candidates.suggestion: Implement the discreet-mode choice and replace this assertion with tests for its default, an explicit choice, and preservation on rerun.
candidates.failure_scenario: A user runs interactive init expecting to configure discreet mode; no question is asked and the test suite accepts the omission.

candidates.title: --yes registers MCP despite the negative default
candidates.detail: The confirmation helper returns true unconditionally under `--yes`, including for MCP registration whose default is false. Thus `--yes` does not accept the displayed default and changes external CLI configuration without the requested affirmative choice. Existing consent tests omit `--yes`, while the empty-init test expects the registration effect.
candidates.suggestion: Have `--yes` select the supplied fallback for confirmations, and test that `--yes` does not register MCP when its default is no.
candidates.failure_scenario: Running `limitless init --yes` on a machine without MCP registrations invokes both CLI registration commands even though the registration prompt defaults to no.

candidates.title: A running daemon does not reload newly written setup configuration
candidates.detail: Service installation is skipped whenever the preflight daemon check is healthy, even when init just wrote new providers, repositories, or merge policy. The service therefore continues using its old in-memory configuration. The partial-config test mocks the service and checks the file rather than the daemon's effective settings.
candidates.suggestion: Reload or restart the service when configuration changes, and test init against a fake service that retains its loaded configuration until reloaded.
candidates.failure_scenario: A healthy daemon is running when init adds a provider and changes the merge default; init reports success, but subsequent daemon operations still use the old configuration.

candidates.title: Init tests replace the production smoke adapter
candidates.detail: The fixture substitutes `d.smoke` with a fixed passing row, so the tests do not exercise the production adapter, its use of the configured paths and environment, or collection of actual smoke failures. This leaves the central requirement to run live smoke checks unverified.
candidates.suggestion: Add a test of the production smoke adapter with fake CLI and HTTP dependencies, verifying that real collected failures appear in the summary and produce a nonzero exit.
candidates.failure_scenario: The production smoke adapter stops collecting rows or runs with the wrong configuration; every init test still receives the fixture's fixed passing result.

candidates.title: Redact smoke retry details before they are truncated
candidates.detail: Smoke rows are redacted only after the smoke runner has constructed retriedAfter by truncating the first failure reason to 200 characters. If truncation cuts through a credential, safe() cannot match the complete credential, and the remaining fragment is written to smoke-last.json and printed in the init summary.
candidates.suggestion: Redact failure reasons before constructing or truncating retry details, including the first-attempt reason.
candidates.failure_scenario: A transient smoke failure includes a configured API key near the 200-character boundary. The retry succeeds, but retriedAfter contains a partial key that is persisted and returned by init.

candidates.title: Check access to repositories supplied to init
candidates.detail: Doctor checks repository access only for the first repository already present in the loaded configuration. The --repo values are processed after doctor finishes, so a fresh init can accept and enable repositories without checking access to any of them. Additional configured repositories are also never checked.
candidates.suggestion: Validate access for every repository that init will enable before writing configuration, and report each configured repository's access in doctor.
candidates.failure_scenario: On a fresh configuration, `limitless init --yes --repo org/private` passes gh auth status even though the account lacks access or SSO authorization for org/private, then writes that repository into configuration.

candidates.title: Discreet mode is never offered or configured
candidates.detail: The request says init asks about “the merge policy, and discreet mode.” The implementation always reports discreet mode as skipped and never asks or persists a choice.
candidates.suggestion: Implement the requested discreet-mode question and configuration, or explicitly revise the requirement if that feature cannot be supported.
candidates.failure_scenario: A user runs init on a fresh installation and has no opportunity to select discreet mode.

candidates.title: Fresh setup does not verify access to the requested repositories
candidates.detail: The request requires gh authentication to have repository access and an SSO read against a configured repository. Doctor checks only the first repository already in config, before init collects --repo or interactive repository choices. A fresh install therefore proceeds without checking any selected repository, and additional configured repositories are never checked.
candidates.suggestion: Check access to each repository selected for setup before writing configuration, and report SSO failures with the requested fix.
candidates.failure_scenario: An authenticated user runs init --yes --repo org/private on an empty config without access or SSO authorization; the check passes and setup writes the repository anyway.

candidates.title: A healthy daemon is left running with stale configuration
candidates.detail: Init writes newly detected providers and repository settings but skips service installation or reload whenever the pre-write doctor saw a healthy daemon. The already running daemon retains its old configuration, so the setup changes do not take effect there.
candidates.suggestion: Safely reload or restart the service when configuration affecting the daemon changes, then wait for health before smoke checks.
candidates.failure_scenario: Init adds a local provider while the daemon is healthy; subsequent daemon runs cannot route to that provider until the service is restarted separately.

candidates.title: OpenAI model lists can be misclassified as Anthropic servers
candidates.detail: The detection treats a first model with type equal to model as proof of an Anthropic-compatible API. The OpenAI model object can also contain type: model, so this heuristic can register an OpenAI endpoint with the Anthropic harness and the wrong base URL.
candidates.suggestion: Probe an endpoint or response characteristic that reliably distinguishes the supported protocols, and avoid registering an ambiguous server under an unverified protocol.
candidates.failure_scenario: A loopback OpenAI-compatible server returns a model list containing {"id":"local","type":"model"}; init registers it as anthropic-compatible and subsequent requests use the wrong protocol.

candidates.title: Configured providers without health_url receive no health check
candidates.detail: The request says every configured provider answers its health check. This loop silently omits health status whenever health_url is absent, even though that field is optional for configured compatible providers.
candidates.suggestion: Provide an appropriate health probe for configured providers or explicitly report that their health cannot be checked with an actionable fix.
candidates.failure_scenario: A configured compatible provider has a base URL but no health_url and its server is down; doctor reports no provider health problem.

candidates.title: Doctor omits the individual last smoke results
candidates.detail: The request says “the last smoke results” are reported. Doctor reduces the stored rows to a pass summary or failed names, omitting individual passed and skipped checks and their reasons.
candidates.suggestion: Include the stored smoke rows, including statuses and useful reasons, in human-readable and JSON output.
candidates.failure_scenario: The last smoke run skipped a backend because credentials were unavailable; doctor says only that the last smoke passed.

candidates.title: --yes changes MCP configuration despite the default being no
candidates.detail: The request says --yes accepts defaults and init asks before changing MCP configuration. The confirmation default is false, but confirm returns true unconditionally under --yes, causing both client configurations to be changed without the stated default being respected.
candidates.suggestion: Have --yes select the actual confirmation default, or provide a separate explicit opt-in for MCP registration.
candidates.failure_scenario: A non-interactive user runs init --yes expecting the default no for MCP registration; init invokes the client MCP add commands.

Verifier: 11 candidates, 11 checked, 0 refuted.

findings.title: Misses signal commands executed through find
findings.detail: The detector stops examining a shell segment after recognizing its first command, so it does not detect a signal command passed to find -exec. A targeted check returned false for `find . -exec kill 123 \;`. The tool call therefore produces neither the requested warning event nor a run.warning feed item.
findings.suggestion: Recognize executable arguments to find -exec and -execdir, with a fixture that distinguishes them from printed text.
findings.failure_scenario: An agent invokes `find . -exec kill 123 \;` to signal a PID; the command is logged without a signal warning.

verification.evidence: src/harness/signals.ts:44: `if (!start) continue;`; src/harness/signals.ts:59: `start = false;`. After recognizing `find`, subsequent `-exec kill` tokens are skipped. A targeted detector probe returned false and emitted zero warnings.
verification.trigger: A shell tool executes `find . -exec kill 123 \;`; the tool call is logged without a signal warning or run.warning feed item.

findings.title: Treats ordinary gate output as a confinement failure
findings.detail: Any output line matching the new signal-confinement expression marks the gate as failed, even when the command exits successfully and confinement was enforced. For example, a test printing `signal confinement unavailable` as an expected diagnostic causes a blocking confinement_error.
findings.suggestion: Propagate confinement failures through a structured result or restrict diagnostic detection to a trusted launcher failure, rather than arbitrary gate output.
findings.failure_scenario: A passing test suite prints `signal confinement unavailable` while testing an expected refusal; the gate is reported as a blocking confinement error.

verification.evidence: src/gates/run.ts:55-60 matches `/signal confinement (?:not|unavailable|preflight|incompatible)/i` anywhere in output. Lines 68,75-76 apply this to both output streams; line 82 sets `ok: !confinementError && res.exitCode === 0 ...`. Lines 195,205 classify matching results as `confinement_error` and blocking. A targeted invocation of compareGates with exitCode:0, ok:true, and output 'PASS: signal confinement unavailable is rejected' returned verdict:'confinement_error', blocking:true.
verification.trigger: A passing gate prints 'signal confinement unavailable', for example in an expected-refusal test name or diagnostic. The ordinary output is mistaken for a confinement failure, blocking the run despite exit status zero.

findings.title: Live harness acceptance checks remain unperformed

findings.title: Miss signal commands executed through common wrappers
findings.detail: The detector stops examining a command segment after its first executable unless that executable is in a small wrapper list. Consequently, signal commands invoked through ordinary utilities produce neither a warning event nor a run.warning feed item. A targeted check, `bun -e 'import {signalCommand} from "./src/harness/signals.ts"; for (const s of ["timeout 5 pkill -f marker", "find . -exec kill 123 \\;"]) console.log(JSON.stringify(s), signalCommand(s))'`, printed `"timeout 5 pkill -f marker" false` and `"find . -exec kill 123 \\;" false`.
findings.suggestion: Recognize signal executables in common command-executing wrappers and add parser fixtures for those forms.

findings.title: Detect PIDs supplied through backtick command substitution
findings.detail: The detector only recognizes kill operands beginning with a digit, dollar sign, or percent sign. A PID supplied through backtick command substitution is therefore missed, so the tool call produces neither a warning event nor a run.warning feed item. The targeted check `bun -e 'import {signalCommand} from "./src/harness/signals.ts"; console.log(signalCommand("kill `cat pid`"))'` returned `false`.
findings.suggestion: Recognize backtick command substitution in kill operands and add a captured tool-call fixture for it.

verification.evidence: src/harness/signals.ts:64–66 requires `name === "kill"` and `(piped || operands.some((t) => /^-?(?:\d+$|[$%])/.test(unquote(t))))`. findings.title: Opaque binaries replacing LFS pointers bypass the binary allowance
findings.detail: The `basePointers` exemption excludes a changed file from `binaryPaths` whenever its base version is a strict LFS pointer, even when the new version is an actual opaque binary. The existing test explicitly expects this exemption for `tracked.dat`. This leaves an edited executable, archive, or other non-media binary unblocked without `Allow: binary`, contrary to the request. The exemption predates the diff, but the requested policy change leaves it in place.
findings.suggestion: Apply the non-inert binary check to actual binary content at HEAD even when the base version was an LFS pointer, and cover that transition with and without the allowance.

The targeted command `bun -e 'import {isForbiddenFormat} from "./src/gates/media.ts"; console.log(isForbiddenFormat("", Buffer.from("const token = \"MZ\";\n")))'` printed `true`.
findings.suggestion: Do not classify arbitrary text as binary based on signatures occurring anywhere in its contents.
findings.failure_scenario: Adding a TypeScript file containing `const token = "MZ";` produces a binary-content block even though its diff is visible.

verification.evidence: src/gates/media.ts:22 defines the MZ signature as `"4d5a"`; line 33 searches the entire buffer with `bytes.includes(magic)`. src/git/repos.ts:835 deletes forbidden paths from `raw`, and lines 953–955 classify non-inert paths absent from raw as binary. src/gates/audit.ts:281–284 emits a blocking finding without the allowance.
verification.trigger: Add a TypeScript file containing `const token = "MZ";`, without Allow: binary → binary-content blocks it. Direct execution of isForbiddenFormat with this exact text returned true.

findings.title: Executable text files require a binary allowance
findings.detail: modeRequiresAllowance is set for every executable file and for mode-only changes, then added to binaryPaths regardless of its content. The request requires an allowance for other binary files, not ordinary visible text or permission changes.
findings.suggestion: Base binary-content findings on the content classification rather than the executable bit or a mode-only change.
findings.failure_scenario: Adding an executable shell script or changing a text script from mode 100644 to 100755 produces a binary-content block.

verification.evidence: src/git/repos.ts:557 sets "modeRequiresAllowance: newMode === \"100755\" || (oldMode !== `:${newMode}` && oldOid === newOid)". src/git/repos.ts:951-952 selects binaryPaths with "({ path, from, modeRequiresAllowance }) => modeRequiresAllowance ||". src/gates/audit.ts:280-284 turns these paths into binary-content blocks without the allowance.
verification.trigger: Add a text shell script with Git mode 100755, or change an existing text script from 100644 to 100755. Either produces a binary-content block without Allow: binary.

findings.title: LFS pointers with source extensions still produce the spurious warning
findings.detail: The request says a new strict LFS pointer under an existing filter=lfs rule produces no warning. Although headTextPaths now uses afterText.text, this branch deliberately retains pointers whose names match SOURCE_PATH in that set, so the warning still occurs for those paths.
findings.suggestion: Exclude strict LFS pointers from the set used for the new-or-moved-files warning regardless of extension.
findings.failure_scenario: Add a strict LFS pointer named data.json under an existing `*.json filter=lfs` rule; it remains in headTextPaths and triggers the warning.

verification.evidence: src/gates/audit.ts:110-111 includes json in SOURCE_PATH. src/git/repos.ts:842 removes a strict pointer from text only when "!SOURCE_PATH.test(path)"; :973 returns "headTextPaths: [...afterText.text]". src/gates/audit.ts:270-275 warns when "existing && headText.has(path) && addedPaths.has(path)".
verification.trigger: Add a strict data.json LFS pointer under an existing *.json filter=lfs rule. Its source extension keeps it in headTextPaths, producing the spurious new/moved-files warning.

findings.title: Valid large images are denied the inert-media exemption
findings.detail: The request says new and edited PNG files pass and does not impose a size limit. Files above 32 MiB are skipped, and the format validators also impose decompressed-size and structure restrictions, so valid images can require an allowance.
findings.suggestion: Honor the requested exemption for the listed media without adding unsupported size or parser restrictions.
findings.failure_scenario: A valid binary PNG larger than 32 MiB is added or edited and receives a binary-content block.

verification.evidence: src/gates/media.ts:5 defines `MEDIA_LIMIT = 32 * 1024 * 1024`. src/git/repos.ts:933 skips exemption validation with `if (!Number.isSafeInteger(size) || size <= 0 || size > MEDIA_LIMIT) continue;`. Consequently, src/git/repos.ts:955 includes the path through `!inert.has(path)`. src/gates/audit.ts:280-284 emits a `binary-content` finding with severity `block` unless `ctx.allow?.includes("binary")`.
verification.trigger: Add or edit a valid binary PNG larger than 32 MiB without Allow: binary. The size guard prevents its inert-media exemption, so the audit blocks media the request requires to pass.

findings.title: Change exceeds the explicit source-line budget

findings.suggestion: Reduce the implementation to the requested classification and LFS changes within the stated source-line budget.

candidates.title: Do not classify readable source as binary from embedded magic strings
candidates.detail: The classifier searches complete text blobs for short format signatures, including the ordinary text 'ustar' and 'MZ', then removes matching files from the text set. findings.title: Descendants that create a new process group survive invocation teardown
findings.detail: Signalling the original process group does not kill descendants that call setsid or otherwise move to another process group. If such a child redirects its standard streams, runProcess returns while it is still running, so it can keep writing during cleanup. A standalone check using runProcess with a forked child that calls setsid and redirects its streams returned {"pid":30121,"aliveAfterReturn":true}.
findings.suggestion: Track and terminate the invocation's descendants independently of their process group, and wait for them before returning or starting cleanup.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer launches a background writer that starts a new session and redirects its streams, then exits or is stopped; the writer survives and can race worktree cleanup.

verification.evidence: src/util/proc.ts:115 signals only the original process group: `process.kill(-child.pid, sig)`. Its fallback at :119 is `child.kill(sig)`, which targets only the immediate child. Neither reaches a descendant in another group. A targeted reproduction spawning a detached descendant returned `{ "exitCode": 0, "descendantAlive": true }`.

The reported binary-content flag did not reproduce: src/git/repos.ts contains no NUL bytes.

findings.title: Children with a replaced environment can survive invocation shutdown
findings.detail: Shutdown selects processes by inherited environment markers. A child started with a fresh, nonempty environment has neither marker and is omitted from the scan, even when it remains in the invocation's process group. The targeted command `bun -e 'import { runProcess } from "./src/util/proc.ts"; const r = await runProcess({cmd:["/bin/sh","-c","/usr/bin/env -i FOO=bar ~/.bun/bin/bun -e '\''setInterval(() => {}, 1000)'\'' >/dev/null 2>&1 & echo $!; /bin/sleep 0.2"],cwd:process.cwd(),env:process.env}); const pid=Number(r.stdout.trim()); let alive=false; try { process.kill(pid,0); alive=true; } catch {} console.log(JSON.stringify({pid,alive,result:r.exitCode})); if(alive) process.kill(pid,"SIGKILL");'` printed `{"pid":73144,"alive":true,"result":0}`. The check terminated its own child afterward.
findings.suggestion: Track and terminate the invocation's process group and descendants independently of environment inheritance, including processes that replace their environment.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer launches a background writer through `env -i FOO=bar` and exits or stalls. Shutdown reports success while the writer continues modifying the worktree during cleanup.

Targeted reproduction returned exitCode 0 with the sanitized-environment child still alive.
verification.trigger: An implementer launches a background writer with env -i FOO=bar and redirected stdio, then exits. Teardown excludes the unmarked writer and returns successfully, allowing cleanup while it remains active.

findings.title: A child that replaces its environment survives invocation teardown
findings.detail: Shutdown identifies descendants through inherited environment markers. A child that starts with a replacement environment containing no marker is omitted, even when it remains in the invocation’s process group, so teardown can report success while the child continues running. On Darwin, the group fallback applies only when the inspected environment is empty; on Linux the group is not used for discovery. A targeted check using `bun -e` to run `/usr/bin/env -i X=1 ~/.bun/bin/bun -e 'setTimeout(()=>{},30000)'` in the background returned `{"pid":83652,"alive":true,"exitCode":0}` after `runProcess` completed. The check then killed the child it started.
findings.suggestion: Track and terminate proven process-group and descendant members independently of inherited environment markers, and fail closed when their termination cannot be confirmed.

findings.title: Environment-scrubbing descendant coverage excludes Linux

findings.title: Linux teardown silently misses descendants that replace their environment
findings.detail: Linux process discovery selects descendants solely by inherited environment markers. A child that executes with a cleared or replaced environment before the first scan is absent from the candidate list, even if it remains in the invocation's process group. Once the direct child exits, two empty scans are treated as confirmation of shutdown, allowing cleanup and subsequent rounds while the descendant remains alive.

findings.failure_scenario: An implementer launches a background writer using env -i and exits or is stopped before teardown discovers the writer. The writer continues changing the worktree after runProcess reports shutdown.

verification.evidence: src/util/proc.ts:101–105 excludes processes without invocation markers. src/util/proc.ts:181 initializes `claimed` only when shutdown starts, and src/util/proc.ts:184–188 populates it from marker discovery. src/util/proc.ts:196 permits successful shutdown with no claimed processes after the direct child exits.
verification.trigger: On Linux, a background writer clears its environment before teardown discovers it and redirects its standard streams. Shutdown completes without detecting or killing the writer, which continues changing the worktree after runProcess resolves.

findings.title: A shared working directory can cause unrelated processes to be killed
findings.detail: The Darwin orphan heuristic treats an environment-hidden process as an invocation member merely because it was born after invocation start, has parent PID 1, and has a cwd under one of the invocation directories. findings.failure_scenario: Another user-launched or factory process with a hidden environment becomes orphaned in the same checkout while a command is running. When that command ends, teardown can terminate the unrelated process.

verification.evidence: src/util/processes-darwin.ts:65–68 returns `directories.some((directory) => path === directory || path.startsWith(...))` after checking orphan status and birth time. Line 197 seeds these processes into `marked`; src/util/proc.ts:206 calls `process.kill(pid, signal)`.
verification.trigger: A same-UID process with a hidden environment becomes orphaned in the shared checkout after invocation start. The shared working directory causes teardown to terminate the unrelated process.

findings.title: Detached descendants can outlive the invocation

findings.detail: Linux process discovery selects only processes carrying an invocation environment marker. A child that starts with a sanitized environment is never claimed, even if it remains in the invocation's process group. Once the parent exits, shutdown can report success while that child continues writing.
findings.suggestion: Track process-group and descendant membership independently of environment markers, and confirm those processes have exited before returning.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer launches a background writer with a sanitized environment, such as through env -i, then exits or is stopped. The writer survives and can race the subsequent worktree cleanup.

candidates.detail: The retry is enabled only for checkoutCommitted's clean -ffdxq. The final discardChanges call uses clean -fdq without retrying it, yet its failure is reported as cleanup failing after retry. A transient failure there unnecessarily fails the round.
candidates.suggestion: Retry the final clean once after a failed implement round and report accurately whether a retry was attempted.
candidates.failure_scenario: A failed implement round reaches final cleanup and git clean -fdq fails once but would succeed on a second attempt.

candidates.title: Linux shutdown misses descendants that replace their environment
candidates.detail: Linux discovery selects processes solely by inherited environment markers. A descendant that starts with a replacement environment before the first shutdown scan is never claimed, even if it remains in the invocation's process group. Shutdown can therefore report success while that process continues writing.
candidates.suggestion: Track process-group and descendant membership independently of environment markers, with identity checks before signaling.
candidates.failure_scenario: On Linux, an implementer starts a background writer with env -i and exits or is stopped. The writer survives runProcess and races with worktree cleanup.

candidates.title: Environment-replacing descendants are only tested on macOS
candidates.detail: The scrubbed-group and scrubbed-ancestry cases are skipped outside Darwin. The cross-platform process tests preserve the invocation markers, so they do not detect Linux returning successfully with an unmarked child still alive.
candidates.suggestion: Add a Linux subprocess case that starts a writer with a replacement environment and verifies it is gone before runProcess returns.
candidates.failure_scenario: A Linux process-tree implementation that ignores all children started with env -i passes the existing applicable tests.

candidates.title: Failed-round cleanup errors outside git clean still fail the run
candidates.detail: The round-failure handler only catches WorktreeCleanError, but checkoutCommitted also removes the index and runs git reset before git clean. Errors from those cleanup steps propagate as ordinary errors and fail the run, contrary to the requested handling of cleanup failure after a failed implement round.
candidates.suggestion: Classify failures across the failed-round cleanup operation as cleanup failures and route them through the round retry or escalation policy.
candidates.failure_scenario: After a stuck implementer, git reset --hard fails because a worktree file cannot be removed; the run fails instead of proceeding to another round or escalating.

candidates.title: Failed-round tests inject clean errors but not reset or index cleanup errors
candidates.detail: The cleanup failure matrix injects failures only for clean commands. It does not exercise failures in the preceding index removal or reset, allowing those failures to escape the round-failure handler and fail the run.
candidates.suggestion: Add a failed-implement case where reset or index removal fails and assert the run retries the round or escalates rather than failing outright.
candidates.failure_scenario: A stuck implementer's git reset fails, but every existing cleanup failure test still passes because its reset succeeds.

candidates.title: Detached children can escape shutdown by replacing their environment
candidates.detail: A reparented process is considered for the cwd fallback only when its environment is entirely hidden. A detached child with an ordinary replacement environment has no marker, parent link, or matching session by the time its parent exits, so shutdown reports success while the child continues running. Linux likewise relies on environment markers. A targeted Bun subprocess check that spawned a detached child with env={PATH: process.env.PATH} printed `escaped child alive: 43017` after runProcess returned; the check then killed its own child.
candidates.suggestion: Track descendants using an ownership mechanism that survives environment replacement and reparenting, or refuse to confirm shutdown when ownership cannot be established.
candidates.failure_scenario: An implementer starts a detached background writer with a scrubbed environment and exits or stalls; the writer survives into worktree cleanup and subsequent rounds.

candidates.title: Cwd and birth time can identify an unrelated process as owned
candidates.detail: An orphan with a hidden environment is treated as an invocation descendant solely because it was born after invocation start and its cwd is under an invocation directory. Those facts do not establish ancestry. The resulting PID is sent SIGTERM and potentially SIGKILL, even when another user process or concurrent factory run created it.
candidates.suggestion: Only signal processes whose ownership is established by a reliable ancestry or isolation mechanism; treat ambiguous processes as an unconfirmed shutdown.
candidates.failure_scenario: An unrelated shell is orphaned in the same worktree while an invocation runs, and macOS exposes its environment as hidden. The invocation's shutdown signals that unrelated shell.

candidates.title: Reset failures during cleanup still fail the run
candidates.detail: checkoutCommitted performs rev-parse and reset before git clean, but only a twice-failed clean becomes WorktreeCleanError. A CommandError from reset propagates through the gates handler and fails the whole run even when implementerIssue records a failed or stuck round.
candidates.suggestion: Classify failures of the complete post-implement cleanup operation as round failures, while retaining the explicit retry for git clean.
candidates.failure_scenario: After a stuck implementer, git reset --hard fails because a tracked worktree file cannot be restored; the run fails instead of retrying the round or escalating it as a round failure.

candidates.title: Descendants that replace their environment can survive on Linux
candidates.detail: The request says to "kill its whole process tree" and that "Background children must not outlive the invocation." Linux discovery selects only processes carrying an inherited environment marker. A descendant that starts with a clean environment before the first shutdown scan is never claimed, even if it remains in the invocation's process group. Shutdown can then be confirmed while that child continues writing.
candidates.suggestion: Track process-group and descendant membership independently of inherited environment markers, with identity checks before signalling.
candidates.failure_scenario: An implementer starts a background writer with env -i and then exits or is stopped. The writer has no marker, survives the scan, and can race with worktree cleanup.

candidates.title: CWD heuristic can terminate an unrelated orphan
candidates.detail: An unmarked orphan is treated as an invocation descendant solely because it was born after invocation start and its current directory is under a scanned root. Neither condition establishes ancestry. The termination loop consequently sends signals to processes that the invocation did not start.
candidates.suggestion: Require verifiable invocation ancestry or another exclusive ownership mechanism before signalling a process.
candidates.failure_scenario: A separate process starts and detaches in the same worktree while an invocation is running. If its environment is hidden and its parent exits, the next shutdown scan can classify and kill it.

candidates.title: Some cleanup failures after a failed round still fail the run
candidates.detail: The request says to "Treat a cleanup failure after a stuck/failed implement round as a round failure" and to "retry the clean once after the kill." Only the first checkout's exact clean -ffdxq command is retried and converted to WorktreeCleanError. A failure in that checkout's reset, or in the later checkout used for a timed-out gate rerun, escapes as a run failure. The finally-block discard's clean -fdq is converted to a round failure but is not retried.
candidates.suggestion: Apply round-failure handling to all cleanup operations following a failed implementation, and retry each applicable clean once before reporting the round failure.
candidates.failure_scenario: After a stuck implementer, git reset --hard fails during checkout, or the first clean -ffdxq in the gate timeout rerun fails transiently. The error bypasses the WorktreeCleanError handler and fails the run instead of advancing to another round.

Reviewed the reader profile, command service, harness integration, and failure paths. The targeted command `bun test test/scratch.test.ts test/verification.test.ts` could not run because the checkout lacks the installed `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` dependency. Live Seatbelt enforcement therefore remains unverified in this environment.

Reviewed the reader profile, verifier integration, and added tests. The targeted command `bun test test/scratch.test.ts test/verification.test.ts` could not run because the checkout lacks the installed `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` dependency; it reported two module-resolution errors before running any tests. I could not verify Seatbelt enforcement in this environment.

Reviewed the reader profile, verifier integration, and command transport. Targeted tests could not run because the checkout lacks the installed MCP SDK dependency; Seatbelt enforcement could therefore not be checked in this environment.

Reviewed the verifier dispatch, both harnesses, reader profile, and added tests. Targeted tests could not start because the MCP SDK is not installed in this checkout. The profile leaves local-service access open and the new command path is macOS-only.

Verifier: 17 candidates, 13 checked, 0 refuted.

findings.title: Reader commands can connect to unrelated local services
findings.detail: The outbound rule permits connections to every loopback TCP port in the ephemeral range, regardless of which process owns the listener. A verifier command can therefore interact with an unrelated local service, including one belonging to another run. This exceeds the requested isolated loopback test access and creates a path to services that may provide external network access or sensitive data.
findings.suggestion: Isolate verifier networking so connections are limited to servers owned by the verification command, or use the option of citing gate results instead.
findings.failure_scenario: Another process listens on 127.0.0.1:50000; a verifier command connects to that service and sends requests under the reader profile.

verification.evidence: src/harness/reader.ts:56: `...portRules("allow network-outbound", "remote", 49152, 65535)`. At line 35, the generated rule checks only `localhost` and the destination port; it does not require the destination listener to belong to the reader.
verification.trigger: An unrelated service listens on 127.0.0.1:50000. A reader command can connect and send requests, crossing the intended network confinement boundary.

findings.title: The profile allows binding fixed loopback ports
findings.detail: The network-bind rule allows every loopback TCP port. Restricting inbound traffic later does not prevent bind itself from reserving a fixed port, so a verifier command can deny a local service the ability to start. The request permits ephemeral ports only.
findings.suggestion: Enforce ephemeral-only binding, or avoid granting the bind capability when that restriction cannot be enforced.
findings.failure_scenario: A verifier command binds 127.0.0.1:12345 and keeps the socket open; another local process cannot bind its service to that port.

verification.evidence: src/harness/reader.ts:54: `'(allow network-bind (local tcp "localhost:*"))'`. The inbound restriction at line 55 applies to listening/receiving, not the preceding bind operation.
verification.trigger: With port 12345 available, a reader command binds 127.0.0.1:12345 and retains the socket without listening, reserving the port and preventing another process from binding it.

findings.title: Workflow modification is outside the authorized scope
findings.detail: The change adds a CI job, but the request does not include the required `Allow: workflows` authorization identified by the audit policy.
findings.suggestion: Remove the workflow modification or obtain the required workflow authorization.
findings.failure_scenario: The change is submitted with the added macOS CI job while the request has no `Allow: workflows` directive.

findings.title: Reader commands can connect to existing local services
findings.detail: The outbound rule permits TCP connections to every loopback port in the ephemeral range, regardless of which process owns the listener. A verifier command can therefore access or modify other local services, including services that expose unauthenticated APIs on dynamically allocated ports. The requested exception was for local test servers while outbound connections remain denied.
findings.suggestion: Isolate test networking so commands can connect only to listeners created within their own confinement boundary, or use the gates-results alternative.
findings.failure_scenario: Another process listens on 127.0.0.1:50000; a verifier command connects to that service and invokes its API.

verification.evidence: src/harness/reader.ts:56 permits `network-outbound` to remote ports 49152–65535. Line 35 generates `(require-all (remote tcp "localhost:*") (remote tcp ...))`, with no listener ownership restriction.
verification.trigger: An existing local API listens on 127.0.0.1:50000. A reader command connects and invokes that API despite the requested outbound-network restriction.

findings.title: Fixed ephemeral-range ports are allowed
findings.detail: The profile permits binding any loopback port and permits listening on every port from 49152 through 65535. Consequently, it does not enforce the requested ephemeral-port-only binding: explicitly selected ports in that range work as well.
findings.suggestion: Enforce allocation through port zero, or choose the gates-results alternative if Seatbelt cannot distinguish it from fixed-port binds.
findings.failure_scenario: A verifier test binds 127.0.0.1:50000 and listens successfully even though it explicitly requested a fixed port.

verification.evidence: src/harness/reader.ts:54 allows binding `localhost:*`; line 55 adds `...portRules("allow network-inbound", "local", 49152, 65535)`. Neither rule distinguishes an explicitly requested port from one allocated through port zero.
verification.trigger: A reader test explicitly binds the available address 127.0.0.1:50000 and listens successfully, bypassing the requested restriction to ephemeral allocations.

findings.title: Reader commands can connect to unrelated loopback services
findings.detail: The profile permits outbound TCP connections to every loopback port from 49152 through 65535. That permits a verifier command to reach an existing local service in that range, despite the requirement that outbound connections stay denied.
findings.suggestion: Restrict connections to listeners created for the verification command, or use the alternative of allowing the verifier to cite gate results if Seatbelt cannot enforce that restriction.
findings.failure_scenario: A separate process listens on 127.0.0.1:50000; a reader command connects to it and exchanges data.

verification.evidence: src/harness/reader.ts:56: `...portRules("allow network-outbound", "remote", 49152, 65535)`. The rule generator at line 35 restricts address and port only, allowing unrelated loopback listeners in that range.
verification.trigger: A separate process listens on 127.0.0.1:50000. A reader command connects and exchanges data with it, crossing the intended network confinement boundary.

findings.title: Fixed listeners in the ephemeral range are permitted
findings.detail: The bind rule permits every loopback port, and the inbound rule permits all ports in the IANA ephemeral range. A command can therefore explicitly bind and listen on a fixed port in that range, although the requested allowance is for ephemeral ports only.
findings.suggestion: Enforce allocation through port zero, or choose the gate-results alternative if the platform cannot distinguish an ephemeral allocation from an explicit bind.
findings.failure_scenario: A verifier command binds 127.0.0.1:50000 and listens successfully, rather than requesting port 0.

verification.evidence: src/harness/reader.ts:54 allows '(allow network-bind (local tcp "localhost:*"))'; line 55 adds '...portRules("allow network-inbound", "local", 49152, 65535)'. These rules include explicitly selected port 50000 and do not check whether bind requested port 0.
verification.trigger: A command explicitly binds an available 127.0.0.1:50000 and listens; both operations are permitted. Runtime reproduction was unavailable because nested Seatbelt startup is denied in this environment.

findings.title: Socket tests miss fixed high ports and pre-existing local services
findings.detail: The fixed-port checks use only port 12345, outside the range the profile allows, and the successful loopback exchange connects only to a listener created by the same test. These cases pass even when fixed listeners and connections to unrelated local services are allowed.
findings.suggestion: Add enforcement tests that attempt an explicit bind in the allowed ephemeral range and connect to a pre-existing loopback service in that range.
findings.failure_scenario: The profile allows a command to bind 127.0.0.1:50000 or connect to an unrelated listener there, while the current fixture still passes.

verification.evidence: test/reader-fixture.ts:115 checks only `denied(lambda: bind("127.0.0.1", 12345), "fixed-port bind/listen")`; line 117 likewise checks connections only to port 12345. src/harness/reader.ts:54 allows `(allow network-bind (local tcp "localhost:*"))`, and lines 55–56 allow inbound and outbound loopback TCP on every port from 49152 through 65535. These rules include 50000 and do not distinguish pre-existing listeners.
verification.trigger: A reader command binds/listens on an available 127.0.0.1:50000 or connects to an unrelated service already listening there. The profile permits it, while the fixture still passes because its fixed-port denial checks use only 12345.

A regression that prevents either adapter from exposing or invoking the tool can leave this acceptance test passing.
findings.suggestion: Add an integration case through the actual verifier dispatch and adapter boundary, using a fake CLI or process runner to exercise tool discovery and invocation without a paid model.
findings.failure_scenario: An adapter stops configuring the reader MCP server, but the manually wrapped fake verifier still calls the server directly and passes.

verification.evidence: test/verification.test.ts:64 directly invokes `withReaderCommands(fixture.spec, verify)`; its fake handler at line 46 calls `callReaderTool(reader, fixture.command)`. test/reader-fixture.ts:30–31 connects directly using `client.connect(new StreamableHTTPClientTransport(new URL(spec.readerCommandUrl)))` and `client.callTool({ name: "command", arguments: { command } })`. Neither production adapter runs in this acceptance test.
verification.trigger: Remove reader setup from runClaude or runCodex: this acceptance test still installs the endpoint itself and calls it directly, so it passes despite broken adapter integration. This is a test coverage gap; current adapter failure is not demonstrated.

findings.detail: The outbound rule permits connections to every loopback TCP service listening on a port from 49152 through 65535. Repository-controlled test code can consequently send requests to those services or use a local proxy to reach the network, despite the requested outbound isolation.
findings.suggestion: Isolate the command and its local servers from unrelated host services, or use the alternative of allowing the verifier to cite gate results when that isolation cannot be enforced.
findings.failure_scenario: A local HTTP proxy or unauthenticated administrative service listens on 127.0.0.1:50000; a verifier executes a repository test that connects to it and sends requests or data.

verification.evidence: src/harness/reader.ts:56 adds '...portRules("allow network-outbound", "remote", 49152, 65535)'. verification.trigger: An unrelated proxy or administrative service listens on 127.0.0.1:50000. Repository commands can connect and exchange data across the intended reader confinement boundary.

findings.title: Confinement probe does not verify network restrictions
findings.detail: The startup probe checks scratch writes, one denied read, and checkout writes, but never checks that non-loopback connections and listeners are denied. The custom backend explicitly skips the normal verification and executes the command as soon as these filesystem checks pass. Thus a profile or platform that enforces those checks but does not enforce the intended network rules runs untrusted test code without confirming outbound isolation.
findings.suggestion: Probe the effective network restrictions in the same sandboxed process before executing the command, and fail closed with a clear confinement error if the checks cannot be confirmed.
findings.failure_scenario: Seatbelt starts and enforces file rules but the network rules are ineffective or unsupported; the filesystem canaries pass and the repository command runs with network access.

verification.evidence: src/harness/reader.ts:123 and :125 supply 'async () => {}' verification callbacks. The actual startup canary at :132 checks scratch writes, denied reads, and checkout writes before 'exec "$@"', with no socket checks. However, :51 explicitly installs '(deny network*)'; the code does not demonstrate that Seatbelt silently ignores it.
verification.trigger: If Seatbelt accepts the profile and enforces filesystem restrictions while silently failing to enforce network restrictions, the filesystem canaries pass and the command executes. That platform behavior is unproven; the missing network canary is established.

findings.title: Verification commands fail on non-macOS hosts
findings.detail: Every tool-enabled readonly verify invocation is routed through this command tool, which unconditionally rejects non-Darwin platforms. Codex's existing reader profile supports platform-specific confinement, so a Linux verifier that previously ran its shell commands now cannot run any command, including tests unrelated to sockets.
findings.suggestion: Provide an equivalent supported confinement backend on other supported platforms, or retain a working reader command path there.
findings.failure_scenario: A Linux run reaches verification with the Codex harness and the verifier calls the reader command tool; execution throws "Reader commands require macOS Seatbelt".

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/context.ts:699 enables `{ loopbackTests: true }` for tool-enabled readonly verification without a platform guard. src/harness/codex.ts:749-750 routes these invocations through `withReaderCommands`; src/harness/codex.ts:724-725 disables `shell_tool`. src/harness/reader.ts:102 explicitly throws: `if (process.platform !== "darwin") throw new ConfinementError("Reader commands require macOS Seatbelt");`.
verification.trigger: On Linux, a tool-enabled Codex verifier calls the reader command tool. Every command throws the Seatbelt error, preventing command-based verification.
